root.stem: A 17-year-old girl has had 3 weeks of fatigue, low-grade fever, and painful swollen wrists and knees with morning stiffness. A red rash covers her cheeks and the bridge of her nose but spares the folds beside her nose, and it flared after a weekend at the beach. She has painless mouth ulcers and sharp chest pain that eases when she leans forward. Echocardiography shows small warty growths on both sides of the mitral valve. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein and red cell casts. Hemoglobin is low with a positive direct Coombs test, platelets are 60,000/mm³, and the partial thromboplastin time is prolonged and does not correct when normal plasma is added. Antinuclear antibody is positive at a high titre. Antibodies to double-stranded DNA and to the Smith antigen are present, antibodies to nucleosomes are present but antibodies to histones are absent, and serum C3 and C4 are low. Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies are also present. A rapid plasma reagin test is positive but the confirmatory treponemal test is negative. C-reactive protein is raised. She has had no tick exposure, skin pustules, eye redness or urinary symptoms, and she takes no regular medicines.
root.oneliner: 17F + 3 weeks of fatigue, fever and painful swollen wrists and knees with morning stiffness + malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, flared after beach sun + painless mouth ulcers + pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward + warty vegetations on both sides of the mitral valve + proteinuria with red cell casts + low hemoglobin with positive Coombs test + low platelets + prolonged partial thromboplastin time not corrected by mixing + high-titre antinuclear antibody + anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith + antinucleosome without antihistone + low C3 and C4 + anti-Ro (SSA) + false-positive rapid plasma reagin + raised C-reactive protein

flared after a weekend at the beach
small warty growths on both sides of the mitral valve
does not correct when normal plasma is added
serum C3 and C4 are low

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An autoimmune disease of many organs, most common in women of childbearing age and in Black women. The clincher: **malar rash that spares the nasolabial folds, with arthritis, serositis, kidney disease, cytopenias and anti-Smith or anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies**.

nodes.q: Which antibody is the most specific for the disease, though present in only a minority of patients?
nodes.note: Anti-double-stranded DNA is also very specific. Both are far more specific than the screening test.

nodes.q: What type of hypersensitivity reaction causes her rash, joint disease and kidney disease?
nodes.note: Antibody-antigen complexes lodge in skin, joints, glomeruli and serosal surfaces, activate complement and attract neutrophils.

nodes.q: Why does she make antibodies against nuclear material in the first place?
nodes.a: Apoptotic cells are cleared poorly, so nuclear antigens such as nucleosomes are exposed to the immune system
nodes.note: Debris from dying cells is the source of the antigens; the antibodies form complexes with it.

nodes.q: A rare inherited deficiency of which early complement protein gives the strongest risk, because clearance of the debris fails?
nodes.note: C2 and C4 deficiency do the same. Complement proteins coat apoptotic cells and immune complexes so that phagocytes can remove them.

nodes.q: Why are her C3 and C4 low?
nodes.a: Immune complexes activate the classical complement pathway and consume them
nodes.note: Low C3 and C4 track active disease, especially kidney disease.

nodes.q: Which drug-related reaction, 1 to 2 weeks after a foreign protein is given, shares this mechanism?
nodes.note: Fever, rash and joint pain with low C3 appear when circulating immune complexes form. A tuberculin skin test and graft-versus-host disease are T-cell (type IV) reactions, peanut allergy is IgE-mediated (type I), and acute rheumatic fever is antibody cross-reactivity (type II).

nodes.q: Her platelet count is 60,000/mm³. How are her platelets destroyed?
nodes.a: Autoantibodies coat the platelets and splenic macrophages remove them (type II hypersensitivity)
nodes.note: Thrombocytopenia is the classic blood finding in lupus. Leukopenia and lymphopenia are common too.

nodes.q: Her hemoglobin is low and the direct Coombs test is positive. Which antibody class coats her red cells?
nodes.note: Warm IgG antibodies bind red cells at body temperature; splenic macrophages remove them, leaving spherocytes. Lupus is a classic secondary cause.

nodes.q: Her rapid plasma reagin test is positive and the treponemal test is negative. Which antibodies explain this?
nodes.note: The reagin test uses cardiolipin as its antigen, so these antibodies give a **biologic false-positive** result. They also bind phospholipid in the clotting assay and prolong the partial thromboplastin time (the lupus anticoagulant).

nodes.q: Despite the prolonged clotting time, which events do these antibodies cause?
nodes.a: Venous and arterial clots and recurrent miscarriage
nodes.note: The prolonged time is an in-vitro effect; in the body the antibodies are prothrombotic.

nodes.q: Which valve lesion does her echocardiogram show?
nodes.note: Sterile warty vegetations on **both surfaces of the valve**, most often the mitral; they can embolize but rarely cause severe valve disease. Her chest pain relieved by leaning forward is pericarditis, the most common cardiac finding.

nodes.q: If she later becomes pregnant, which heart problem can her anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies cause in the baby?
nodes.note: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and damages the fetal atrioventricular node; the block is permanent. The baby may also have a transient photosensitive rash. Anti-Ro is shared with Sjogren syndrome.

nodes.q: Which organ involvement most worsens the prognosis?
nodes.note: Proteinuria and red cell casts. The leading causes of death are kidney failure, infection, and accelerated coronary atherosclerosis.

nodes.q: Which class of lupus nephritis is both the most common and the most serious?
nodes.note: Nephritic picture. **Wire-loop capillaries** from subendothelial immune complex deposits, with granular IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q on immunofluorescence (a full-house pattern).

nodes.q: Prednisone is added for her nephritis. Where does its receptor sit?
nodes.a: In the cytosol; the drug-receptor complex then moves into the nucleus
nodes.note: The complex acts as a transcription factor and switches off genes for inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor.

nodes.q: If her biopsy had instead shown thick capillary walls with subepithelial deposits and she had nephrotic-range proteinuria, which class would it be?
nodes.note: The nephrotic pattern of lupus nephritis, the most common nephrotic cause in lupus. Class IV is nephritic with subendothelial deposits.

nodes.q: Her C-reactive protein (CRP) is raised. Which organ makes it?
nodes.note: Interleukin-6 from macrophages drives the liver to make acute-phase proteins such as CRP and fibrinogen. In lupus the CRP is often only mildly raised even when the sedimentation rate is high; a big rise suggests serositis or infection.

nodes.q: Which antibody test is positive in nearly all patients, making it the best screening test?
nodes.note: Positive in nearly all patients, so a negative result makes lupus unlikely; a positive result alone is not specific.

nodes.q: Which antibody titre rises with nephritis flares, as C3 and C4 fall?
nodes.note: Follow it with complement levels and urinalysis to track activity.

nodes.q: Which drug is given to nearly every patient to reduce flares?
nodes.note: Add sun protection and NSAIDs for mild disease. It needs yearly eye examinations for retinal toxicity. Organ-threatening disease such as nephritis needs glucocorticoids with mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide.

nodes.q: Her knee pain, fever and anemia could suggest juvenile idiopathic arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: In the systemic form: **quotidian spiking fever + fleeting salmon-colored rash + joint swelling**; no kidney disease, no anti-Smith or anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, complement normal
**Malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds + mouth ulcers + proteinuria with red cell casts + low platelets + anti-Smith or anti-double-stranded DNA**

nodes.note: The trap: both give fever, rash, joint pain and anemia in a young person.

nodes.q: Her swollen knees could suggest Lyme disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tick exposure in an endemic area + expanding erythema migrans + large-joint (knee) arthritis**; positive Borrelia serology; no mouth ulcers or cytopenias
**Symmetric small-joint arthritis + photosensitive malar rash + serositis + nephritis + autoantibodies**; no tick exposure

nodes.q: Her swollen joints could suggest gonococcal arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Sexually active young adult. **Migratory tenosynovitis + vesiculopustular skin lesions + purulent joint fluid** with gram-negative diplococci; treated with ceftriaxone
**Non-purulent, symmetric arthritis + malar rash + nephritis + autoantibodies**; no pustules, no urinary symptoms

nodes.q: Her knee pain could suggest reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter syndrome). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Weeks after a urinary or bowel infection. **Asymmetric lower-limb arthritis + urethritis + conjunctivitis**; HLA-B27 positive, with sacroiliitis
**Symmetric arthritis + malar rash + serositis + proteinuria + anti-Smith**; no eye or urinary symptoms

nodes.q: Her facial rash with joint pain could suggest psoriatic arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Silvery scaly plaques + nail pitting + dactylitis** (sausage digit) with distal finger joint disease; rheumatoid factor negative
**Photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds + visceral involvement (kidney, serosa) + low complement**

nodes.q: Her antinuclear antibodies could suggest drug-induced lupus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: After **hydralazine, procainamide or isoniazid**: **antihistone antibodies** with fever, arthritis and serositis; kidney and brain spared; resolves when the drug stops
**No drug trigger + nephritis + anti-Smith or anti-double-stranded DNA + low complement**; antibodies to nucleosomes but not to histones

nodes.note: She takes no regular medicines and her histone antibodies are absent.

root.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had 3 days of migratory joint pain, and today she cannot walk because of a swollen, painful right knee. At age 12 and again at age 16 she had meningococcal bacteremia, and she has never had any other serious infection. Joint fluid from the right knee contains 50,000 leukocytes/mm³, and Gram stain of the joint fluid and of a cervical swab shows gram-negative diplococci. Her immunoglobulin levels, neutrophil function tests and CD4+ T cell count are normal, and C3 and C4 levels are normal. Her total hemolytic complement activity (CH50) is only 5% of normal.
root.oneliner: 24F + migratory joint pain and a swollen right knee + two prior episodes of meningococcal bacteremia and no other serious infection + gram-negative diplococci in joint fluid and cervix + normal immunoglobulins, neutrophil function and CD4+ T cells + normal C3 and C4 + total hemolytic complement 5% of normal
highlight: At age 12 and again at age 16
never had any other serious infection
immunoglobulin levels, neutrophil function tests and CD4+ T cell count are normal
C3 and C4 levels are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inherited complement defect. The clincher: **repeated Neisseria infections in an otherwise healthy person with almost no total hemolytic complement activity but normal C3 and C4**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Exam options also write it as deficiency of the terminal components of complement.

nodes.q: Which complement proteins can be missing?
nodes.a: Any one of C5 through C9
nodes.note: Usually autosomal recessive; one component is enough to break the chain. C3 and C4 are normal because the early pathway is intact.

nodes.q: What do these proteins build together on a bacterial surface?
nodes.a: The membrane attack complex, a pore that lyses the cell
nodes.note: Without the pore, the classical, alternative and lectin pathways all stop short of killing; opsonization with C3b still works.

nodes.q: Why do the infections involve mainly Neisseria?
nodes.a: Neisseria are killed mainly by complement lysis in the blood; opsonization and phagocytosis alone do not clear them
nodes.note: Meningococcus and gonococcus are the classic pathogens; other bacteria are handled normally because opsonization by C3b and antibody is intact.

nodes.q: Which infection of her knee and cervix did the same defect cause?
nodes.note: Septic arthritis with tenosynovitis from Neisseria gonorrhoeae in a young adult. Treat with ceftriaxone.

nodes.q: Her total hemolytic complement activity (CH50) is only 5% of normal. Which part of the cascade does this test check?
nodes.a: The whole classical pathway, from C1 through the membrane attack complex
nodes.note: Antibody-coated sheep red cells lyse only if every component is present. A near-zero value with normal C3 and C4 points to a terminal defect.

nodes.q: Which preventive measure is given to these patients?
nodes.a: Meningococcal vaccination (with antibiotic prophylaxis during exposure)
nodes.note: Vaccines still work because they make antibody, but the antibody cannot finish the kill, so protection is partial.

nodes.q: Which drug that blocks C5 produces the same risk?
nodes.note: It is used in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome; patients must be vaccinated against meningococcus first.

nodes.q: Her recurrent infections could suggest C3 deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Severe recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, Haemophilus) + glomerulonephritis**; C3 level is low as well as total hemolytic complement
**Only Neisseria infections + normal C3 and C4 + near-absent total hemolytic complement**

nodes.note: The trap: both have a very low total hemolytic complement activity.

nodes.q: Her bacterial infections could suggest Bruton agammaglobulinemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Boy after 6 months of age. **Recurrent sinopulmonary infections + absent B cells + very low IgG, IgA and IgM**; absent tonsils
**Normal immunoglobulins and B cells + only Neisseria infections**; low total hemolytic complement

nodes.q: Her infections could suggest chronic granulomatous disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Catalase-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia)** + granulomas + abnormal dihydrorhodamine test; neutrophil oxidative burst fails
**Neisseria only + normal neutrophil function**; low total hemolytic complement

nodes.q: A low complement level could also suggest C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Recurrent non-itchy swelling of the face, larynx and bowel without hives + low C4**; no excess infections
**Recurrent Neisseria infections + normal C4 + near-absent total hemolytic complement**

root.stem: A 6-month-old boy has had thrush that will not clear, chronic diarrhea, poor weight gain, and a recent pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii. His mother's brother died of overwhelming infection in infancy. A chest radiograph shows no thymic shadow, and the blood lymphocyte count is very low with almost no T cells. His platelet count is normal and he has no eczema. His own bone marrow cells are collected, a retrovirus carrying the normal gene is put into them, and they are returned to him. He does well, but 30 months later he develops a leukemia of T lymphocytes that are all the same clone.
root.oneliner: 6M + persistent thrush, chronic diarrhea, poor weight gain and Pneumocystis pneumonia + maternal uncle died of infection in infancy + no thymic shadow + very low lymphocyte count with almost no T cells + normal platelets, no eczema + retroviral gene therapy, then monoclonal T-cell leukemia at 30 months
highlight: mother's brother died of overwhelming infection in infancy
platelet count is normal and he has no eczema

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Failure of adaptive immunity from the first months of life. The clincher: **severe viral, fungal and bacterial infections in early infancy with absent T cells and no thymic shadow**.

nodes.q: Why is he prone to viral and fungal as well as bacterial infections?
nodes.a: T cells are missing, and B cells cannot make antibody without T-cell help
nodes.note: So cell-mediated and humoral immunity both fail. Infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii and Candida (opportunists) is typical.

nodes.q: His mother's brother died in infancy. Which gene is mutated in the X-linked form?
nodes.a: IL2RG, the common gamma chain shared by receptors for interleukin-2, -4, -7, -9, -15 and -21
nodes.note: Loss of interleukin-7 signaling stops T-cell development. Mutations in JAK3, which signals downstream of the same chain, cause an autosomal recessive form with the same picture.

nodes.q: Besides his X-linked form, which purine salvage enzyme deficiency causes an autosomal recessive form?
nodes.note: Deoxyadenosine and deoxyadenosine triphosphate build up and poison lymphocytes by inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase. Treated with stem cell transplant or enzyme replacement (pegylated adenosine deaminase).

nodes.q: Which newborn screening test picks up the disease?
nodes.note: Low circles mean few new T cells leaving the thymus.

nodes.q: What is the definitive treatment?
nodes.note: Meanwhile: Pneumocystis prophylaxis, immunoglobulin replacement, and **no live vaccines**. Give irradiated blood products to prevent graft-versus-host disease.

nodes.q: Why did retroviral gene therapy lead to a monoclonal T-cell leukemia?
nodes.a: The retrovirus integrated next to a proto-oncogene and switched it on (insertional mutagenesis)
nodes.note: The vector inserts randomly into the genome; a hit next to an oncogene such as LMO2 lets one cell proliferate without control. Clonality shows one cell began the leukemia.

nodes.q: His infections could suggest chronic granulomatous disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Catalase-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus)** + granulomas + normal lymphocyte counts; abnormal dihydrorhodamine test from NADPH oxidase deficiency
**Absent T cells + no thymic shadow + Pneumocystis and thrush** in an infant; NADPH oxidase intact

nodes.note: The trap: both present in infancy with severe infections.

nodes.q: He is a boy with an X-linked family history. How do you tell him from Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?

split.note: **Eczema + small platelets with thrombocytopenia + recurrent infections** in a boy; T cells present at first and fall over time
**Normal platelets, no eczema, absent T cells, no thymic shadow**

nodes.q: His failure to thrive and a purine enzyme defect could suggest Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase. **Self-mutilation + dystonia + hyperuricemia and gout**; infections are not increased
Adenosine deaminase deficiency (another purine enzyme): **severe infections + absent T cells**; no neurological self-injury

nodes.q: His recurrent infections could suggest X-linked agammaglobulinemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Starts after 6 months as maternal IgG fades. **Recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections + absent B cells + very low immunoglobulins**; T cells and thymus normal
**Fungal, viral and Pneumocystis infections + absent T cells + no thymic shadow**

root.stem: A 27-year-old woman returns for a check-up 2 months after a cesarean delivery. She has no fever, and the incision has healed without drainage. A firm, painless, 2-cm subcutaneous nodule lies next to the scar. The nodule is resected. Microscopy shows fibrous connective tissue, macrophages, multinucleated giant cells with nuclei scattered at random, fibroblasts, a few lymphocytes, and scattered fragments of material that shine under polarized light. There is no caseous necrosis and no pus.
root.oneliner: 27F + 2 months after cesarean delivery + firm painless subcutaneous nodule beside the scar + no fever, no drainage + macrophages, multinucleated giant cells and fibroblasts around polarizable fragments + no caseation, no pus
highlight: firm, painless, 2-cm subcutaneous nodule lies next to the scar
multinucleated giant cells with nuclei scattered at random
fragments of material that shine under polarized light
no caseous necrosis and no pus

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A chronic inflammatory reaction around retained material at a wound. The clincher: **a nodule at a surgical site with multinucleated giant cells around polarizable foreign material**.

nodes.q: Which cell fuses to make the giant cells?
nodes.note: Macrophages that cannot swallow the particle fuse into foreign body giant cells, with nuclei scattered at random rather than in a ring.

nodes.q: Why is the material walled off instead of cleared?
nodes.a: Macrophages cannot digest it, so chronic inflammation persists and fibrosis surrounds it
nodes.note: Common sources are suture, talc, silicone or a retained splinter. Polarized light shows the birefringent fragments.

nodes.q: Which macrophage-derived factor drives the fibroblast migration and proliferation that forms the nodule?
nodes.note: It also stimulates collagen deposition and fibrosis. Interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor drive early inflammation and fever, and C3a raises vascular permeability, but none is the chief fibroblast stimulus.

nodes.q: What is the treatment if the nodule is bothersome?
nodes.a: Excision of the nodule with the retained material
nodes.note: Small asymptomatic ones can be observed.

nodes.q: A firm nodule next to a scar could suggest a keloid. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Excess thick collagen bundles that grow beyond the original wound edge**; more common in darker skin; no giant cells or foreign material
**Giant cells around polarizable material** at the site; confined to the surgical track

nodes.note: The trap: both form a firm nodule at a healed surgical scar.

nodes.q: The granulomatous inflammation could suggest sarcoidosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Non-caseating granulomas of epithelioid cells with Schaumann and asteroid bodies**, in lungs and nodes (bilateral hilar adenopathy); no identifiable foreign material
**Localized to a prior wound + polarizable fragments + giant cells with random nuclei**

nodes.q: A nodule next to a recent incision could suggest an abscess. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Warm, tender, fluctuant swelling with fever, filled with neutrophils and pus**; early after surgery
**Painless, firm, no fever or pus; macrophages, giant cells and fibrosis**

nodes.q: Her giant cells could suggest tuberculosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Caseous necrosis in the center + Langhans giant cells with nuclei in a horseshoe at the edge** + acid-fast bacilli
**Non-caseating; giant cells with random nuclei around polarizable material**

root.stem: A newborn boy delivered at term has full cheeks, low-set ears, a small chin and a cleft palate. A right-sided aortic arch is seen on imaging. On day 2 he has a seizure, and the serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels are low. A chest radiograph shows no thymic shadow, and his blood T-cell count is low.
root.oneliner: Newborn M + full cheeks, low-set ears, small chin, cleft palate + right-sided aortic arch + seizure on day 2 with low calcium and low parathyroid hormone + no thymic shadow, low T cells
highlight: full cheeks, low-set ears, a small chin and a cleft palate
serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels are low

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A congenital deletion syndrome. The clincher: **a newborn with a conotruncal heart or arch defect, low calcium and no thymus, with a small chin and low-set ears**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Velocardiofacial syndrome is the same deletion with more palate and speech problems and a milder immune defect.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Fluorescence in situ hybridization or chromosomal microarray for the deletion
nodes.note: Usually a new (de novo) deletion; when inherited it is autosomal dominant.

nodes.q: Which embryologic structures fail to form?
nodes.a: The third and fourth pharyngeal (branchial) pouches
nodes.note: The first and second arches, grooves and pouches are not the problem.

nodes.q: Which cell population, damaged by the deletion, explains the heart and face findings as well?
nodes.note: They migrate into the pharyngeal arches and the aortic outflow tract.

nodes.q: Which type of heart defect is typical?
nodes.a: Conotruncal outflow defects, such as truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot and interrupted aortic arch
nodes.note: His right-sided aortic arch belongs to this group.

nodes.q: Which glands from these pouches are missing, causing his seizure on day 2?
nodes.note: No parathyroid hormone means hypocalcemia: tetany, seizures and a long QT interval. The third pouch makes the inferior parathyroids (and the thymus); the fourth pouch makes the superior parathyroids.

nodes.q: How is the low calcium treated?
nodes.note: Check parathyroid hormone, calcium and magnesium; manage the heart defect surgically.

nodes.q: Which kinds of infection is he at risk for, given no thymic shadow?
nodes.a: Viral, fungal and Pneumocystis infections, from low T-cell immunity
nodes.note: B cells are present but depend on T-cell help. Give irradiated blood products and avoid live vaccines. Complete absence of the thymus needs a thymus transplant.

nodes.q: Which psychiatric disorder is he at higher risk of as a young adult?
nodes.note: Roughly a quarter of adults with the deletion develop a psychotic disorder; learning difficulties are common. Memory aid CATCH-22: Cardiac defects, Abnormal face, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia, chromosome 22.

nodes.q: His small chin and low-set ears could suggest Treacher Collins syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: First and second arch defect (TCOF1). **Malar hypoplasia + downslanting eyes + conductive hearing loss**; heart, calcium and thymus normal
**Third and fourth pouch defect + low calcium + absent thymus + heart outflow defect**

nodes.note: The trap: both have a small chin and low-set ears.

nodes.q: His small chin and cleft palate could suggest Pierre Robin sequence. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Micrognathia, posteriorly placed tongue (glossoptosis) and U-shaped cleft palate**, with airway obstruction; normal calcium, thymus and heart
**Right-sided aortic arch + hypocalcemic seizure + absent thymus** along with the small chin

nodes.q: A newborn with ear changes, a heart defect and low calcium could suggest CHARGE syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: CHD7 mutation. **Coloboma + choanal atresia + genital hypoplasia + ear anomalies + heart defect**, with growth retardation
**22q11.2 deletion + cleft palate + absent thymus + low parathyroid hormone**; no coloboma or choanal atresia

root.stem: A 3-year-old girl has had 2 weeks of diarrhea and low-grade fever. Her lymph nodes are enlarged all over her body, and a CT scan shows enlarged mesenteric and para-aortic nodes. A lymph node biopsy shows sheets of histiocytes and many segmented neutrophils, no granulomas, and numerous acid-fast bacilli later identified as Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare. Serum IgA, IgG and IgM, and B-cell and T-cell counts, are normal. Tests for HIV infection and the dihydrorhodamine oxidative burst test are normal. Serum interferon-gamma level is high.
root.oneliner: 3F + 2 weeks of diarrhea and low-grade fever + generalized lymphadenopathy, mesenteric and para-aortic nodes + biopsy: sheets of histiocytes, many neutrophils, no granulomas, numerous acid-fast bacilli (Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare) + normal immunoglobulins, B and T cells + negative HIV, normal oxidative burst + high serum interferon-gamma
highlight: sheets of histiocytes and many segmented neutrophils
IgA, IgG and IgM, and B-cell and T-cell counts, are normal
Tests for HIV infection and the dihydrorhodamine oxidative burst test are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inherited defect that leaves the body unable to control mycobacteria; one of the Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease disorders, which also cause spreading infection after the live BCG vaccine. The clincher: **disseminated atypical mycobacterial infection in a child with normal immunoglobulins and lymphocytes, no granulomas, and a high interferon-gamma level**.

nodes.q: Which cell can no longer be switched on to kill the mycobacteria it has swallowed?
nodes.note: T helper 1 cells and natural killer cells release interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages to kill intracellular organisms. Without the receptor, the cytokine builds up (high serum level) and the macrophages stay inactive.

nodes.q: Why are there no granulomas on her biopsy?
nodes.a: Inactive macrophages cannot organize into granulomas, so they fill with bacilli instead
nodes.note: Compare with a normal host, in which activated macrophages wall off the organism in granulomas.

nodes.q: Which cytokine from macrophages and dendritic cells normally tells T helper 1 cells to make interferon-gamma?
nodes.note: Defects of interleukin-12 or its receptor give the same infections, but interferon-gamma levels are low and interferon-gamma treatment helps.

nodes.q: How is the infection treated?
nodes.a: A macrolide (clarithromycin or azithromycin) plus ethambutol, often with rifabutin
nodes.note: Complete receptor deficiency needs bone marrow transplantation; interferon-gamma injections help only when some receptor function remains.

nodes.q: Her infection and normal immunoglobulins could suggest chronic granulomatous disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Catalase-positive bacteria and fungi (Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia) with granulomas + abnormal dihydrorhodamine test** because NADPH oxidase is missing
**Mycobacteria with no granulomas + normal oxidative burst + high interferon-gamma level**

nodes.note: The trap: both have recurrent infections with normal antibodies.

nodes.q: The many neutrophils could suggest leukocyte adhesion deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Delayed umbilical cord separation + no pus + very high blood neutrophil count** with bacterial skin and gum infections; defective integrin (CD18)
**Neutrophils reach the node normally; the problem is intracellular mycobacteria**

nodes.q: Disseminated Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare is typical of AIDS. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Positive HIV test + CD4+ T-cell count below 50/mm³** in an adult or child with HIV; granulomas poorly formed
**Negative HIV test + normal CD4+ T-cell count + high interferon-gamma level**

root.stem: A 40-year-old woman has had 6 months of dry mouth, difficulty swallowing dry food, and itching and burning of both eyes as if there is sand in them. She has had several new dental cavities. Examination shows red irritated corneas and conjunctivae, enlarged, firm parotid glands on both sides, and very little saliva. A strip of filter paper under the lower eyelid wets only 3 mm in 5 minutes. Antinuclear antibody is positive and rheumatoid factor is elevated. She is told that she is at higher risk of lymphoma.
root.oneliner: 40F + 6 months of dry mouth and gritty burning eyes + new dental cavities + red corneas and conjunctivae + bilateral firm parotid enlargement + little saliva + filter paper wets 3 mm in 5 minutes + positive antinuclear antibody and elevated rheumatoid factor + at risk of lymphoma
highlight: itching and burning of both eyes
enlarged, firm parotid glands on both sides

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An autoimmune disease of the tear and saliva glands, mostly in middle-aged women. The clincher: **dry eyes + dry mouth with new cavities + bilateral parotid enlargement + positive antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Primary Sjogren syndrome presents alone; the secondary form accompanies another disease such as rheumatoid arthritis.

nodes.q: Which more specific antibody is positive in most patients?
nodes.note: Anti-La (SSB) is less frequent but more specific. Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody are often positive too.

nodes.q: Which fetal complication can these antibodies cause in a pregnancy?
nodes.note: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and damages the fetal conduction system.

nodes.q: What destroys the glands?
nodes.a: Lymphocytic infiltration, mostly CD4+ T cells, with fibrosis of the lacrimal and salivary glands
nodes.note: A type IV (T-cell) injury, with B-cell activation giving autoantibodies.

nodes.q: Which mode of inheritance best describes her risk of this disease?
nodes.note: HLA-DR3 predisposition plus environmental triggers; it does not follow a Mendelian pattern.

nodes.q: Which type of lymphoma is she at risk for?
nodes.a: Marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), often in the parotid
nodes.note: Suspect it when a gland enlarges, becomes hard, or ulcerates, or when cryoglobulins and low C4 appear.

nodes.q: Which bedside test confirms low tear production?
nodes.a: Schirmer test (wetting under 5 mm in 5 minutes)
nodes.note: Her filter paper wets 3 mm.

nodes.q: Which biopsy shows the gland injury?
nodes.a: Minor salivary gland biopsy of the lip, showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis
nodes.note: Used when serology is negative or the diagnosis is uncertain.

nodes.q: Which drug class increases saliva production?
nodes.note: They stimulate muscarinic M3 receptors on the glands. Add artificial tears and dental care; avoid anticholinergic drugs.

nodes.q: Her enlarged parotids and dry eyes could suggest sarcoidosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bilateral hilar adenopathy + uveitis + non-caseating granulomas + raised angiotensin-converting enzyme**; parotid enlargement with facial palsy and fever (Heerfordt syndrome)
**Months of dry eyes and mouth + dental cavities + positive antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor + Schirmer wetting 3 mm**; lymphocytic gland infiltrate, no granulomas

nodes.note: The trap: both enlarge the parotids and dry the eyes.

nodes.q: Her enlarged parotids could suggest mumps. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Unvaccinated child. **Acute painful parotid swelling + fever**, with orchitis or meningitis; paramyxovirus; raised amylase; self-limited
**Months of gradual painless gland swelling + dry eyes and mouth + anti-Ro**

nodes.q: Her elevated rheumatoid factor could suggest rheumatoid arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Symmetric small-joint (hand) arthritis with morning stiffness + anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies**; sicca symptoms only as a secondary feature
**Predominant dry eyes and mouth + parotid swelling + anti-Ro (SSA)**; no erosive arthritis

root.stem: A 43-year-old man has had 1 month of chronic sinus congestion with crusting and occasional nosebleeds. He now has a cough, and his blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg. A chest radiograph shows an infiltrate in the left upper lobe. Serum creatinine is elevated and urinalysis shows blood, protein and red cell casts. Cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are present, while antinuclear antibodies and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are absent. He has no asthma and his eosinophil count is normal.
root.oneliner: 43M + 1 month of sinus congestion, nasal crusting and nosebleeds + cough with left upper lobe infiltrate + hypertension, high creatinine, hematuria and red cell casts + cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies positive + antinuclear and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies negative + no asthma, normal eosinophils
highlight: chronic sinus congestion with crusting and occasional nosebleeds
infiltrate in the left upper lobe
blood, protein and red cell casts
Cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are present
anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are absent
no asthma and his eosinophil count is normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A small-vessel vasculitis of the upper airway, lungs and kidneys. The clincher: **upper airway disease (sinus and nasal) + lung lesions + glomerulonephritis + cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (c-ANCA)**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The same disease under its older eponym.

nodes.q: Against which antigen are his c-ANCA directed?
nodes.note: A neutrophil granule enzyme. Compare p-ANCA, which targets myeloperoxidase.

nodes.q: What does a biopsy of the nose or lung show?
nodes.note: Granulomas with giant cells, necrosis and inflammation of small and medium vessels.

nodes.q: What does his kidney biopsy show?
nodes.note: Little immune complex deposition; crescents explain the rapid fall in kidney function.

nodes.q: Which nasal deformity can follow years of untreated disease?
nodes.note: Destruction of nasal cartilage. Subglottic stenosis is another late airway problem.

nodes.q: How is the diagnosis confirmed?
nodes.a: Biopsy of an affected site (kidney, lung or nose) with ANCA testing
nodes.note: Chest imaging may show nodules or cavities.

nodes.q: How is remission induced?
nodes.note: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 antibody. Maintenance uses rituximab, azathioprine or methotrexate.

nodes.q: Which bladder toxicity of cyclophosphamide is prevented with mesna?
nodes.note: Its metabolite acrolein injures the bladder wall; cyclophosphamide also raises bladder cancer risk.

nodes.q: His kidney and lung disease could suggest microscopic polyangiitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **p-ANCA against myeloperoxidase + necrotizing vasculitis without granulomas**; little or no nose and sinus disease; lung capillaritis
**Sinus and nasal disease + granulomas + c-ANCA against proteinase 3**

nodes.note: The trap: both give pauci-immune kidney failure and lung bleeding, and both are ANCA-positive.

nodes.q: His lung infiltrate and vasculitis could suggest eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Asthma + high eosinophil count + neuropathy (wrist or foot drop)** with p-ANCA in about half; eosinophil-rich granulomas
**No asthma + normal eosinophils + c-ANCA + nose and sinus destruction**

nodes.q: His lung disease with kidney failure could suggest Goodpasture syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies + hemoptysis with glomerulonephritis**; linear IgG deposits on immunofluorescence; no sinus disease
**Anti-glomerular basement membrane negative + c-ANCA + sinus disease**; pauci-immune on immunofluorescence

nodes.q: His lung nodule could suggest lymphomatoid granulomatosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Epstein-Barr virus-driven B-cell proliferation. **Lung nodules + skin and brain lesions + atypical lymphoid cells around vessels**; ANCA negative; no kidney disease
**Nose, lung and kidney disease + c-ANCA + necrotizing vasculitis with granulomas**

nodes.q: The vasculitis with granulomas could suggest temporal arteritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Over age 50. **New headache + jaw claudication + visual loss + high erythrocyte sedimentation rate**; granulomatous inflammation of large and medium arteries, ANCA negative
**Small vessels of nose, lung and glomeruli + c-ANCA**; no headache or jaw pain

root.stem: A 2-year-old boy has had repeated skin abscesses and a staphylococcal bone infection since the age of 4 weeks, and he is now in hospital with pneumonia caused by Aspergillus fumigatus. Draining a swollen lymph node in his armpit released thick pus, and his liver and spleen are enlarged. His hair and skin color match his parents'. Immunoglobulin levels, including immunoglobulin E (IgE), are normal, as are his platelet and neutrophil counts, and his calcium level and heart examination are normal. A human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) test is negative. His maternal uncle died of a severe infection in childhood. In the laboratory, his neutrophils engulf bacteria normally and kill Lactobacillus but not Staphylococcus aureus, and a yellow dye-reduction test shows no color change.
root.oneliner: 2M + abscesses and bone infection since 4 weeks + Aspergillus pneumonia + pus from armpit node + enlarged liver and spleen + normal hair and skin color + normal immunoglobulins, platelets, neutrophils, calcium, heart + HIV test negative + maternal uncle died of infection + neutrophils engulf bacteria, kill Lactobacillus but not S. aureus + no dye color change
highlight: hair and skin color match his parents'
Immunoglobulin levels, including immunoglobulin E (IgE), are normal
platelet and neutrophil counts, and his calcium level and heart examination are normal
human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) test is negative
maternal uncle died of a severe infection
kill Lactobacillus but not Staphylococcus aureus

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inherited failure of phagocytes to kill certain microbes after swallowing them. The clincher: **repeated abscesses from catalase-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus) + neutrophils that engulf but cannot kill + a dye test that stays colorless**.

nodes.q: Which yellow dye test stays colorless because his neutrophils make no oxidants?
nodes.note: Normal neutrophils reduce the yellow dye to blue when they make superoxide; his stay yellow. The dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry test is the modern, more sensitive version and is now preferred to confirm the diagnosis.

nodes.q: Which enzyme is missing?
nodes.note: The enzyme of the phagocyte respiratory burst, which sits in the phagolysosome membrane.

nodes.q: Which product of this enzyme can his neutrophils not make?
nodes.note: Superoxide is turned into hydrogen peroxide by superoxide dismutase, and myeloperoxidase then turns hydrogen peroxide and chloride into hypochlorous acid (bleach), which kills the microbe.

nodes.q: Which metabolic pathway supplies the NADPH that this enzyme uses?
nodes.a: The pentose phosphate pathway (hexose monophosphate shunt)
nodes.note: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is its rate-limiting enzyme, so very severe G6PD deficiency can give a similar killing defect.

nodes.q: How is the disease most often inherited?
nodes.note: Mutations of the gp91phox gene (CYBB) on the X chromosome affect boys, which fits his maternal uncle. Girls are affected through the autosomal recessive forms.

nodes.q: Which step of phagocytosis fails in his neutrophils?
nodes.note: Chemotaxis and ingestion are normal; the oxidative burst that kills the engulfed microbe is absent.

nodes.q: Which tissue lesions form when macrophages cannot clear the microbes?
nodes.note: Macrophages wall off organisms they cannot kill, producing granulomas and lymph node, liver and spleen enlargement. Granulomas can block the gastric outlet or the urinary tract, or mimic Crohn disease in the bowel.

nodes.q: His neutrophils kill Lactobacillus but not Staphylococcus aureus. Which bacterial enzyme explains the difference?
nodes.note: Catalase breaks down the microbe's own hydrogen peroxide, so the neutrophil cannot borrow it to make bleach. Catalase-negative bacteria (Lactobacillus, streptococci, the pneumococcus, enterococci) leave their hydrogen peroxide intact and are killed. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen; other classic catalase-positive organisms are Serratia, Burkholderia cepacia, Nocardia, Aspergillus and Candida.

nodes.q: Which infection is the leading cause of death in this disease?
nodes.note: Aspergillus fumigatus is catalase-positive and, like his pneumonia, usually enters through the lungs.

nodes.q: Which drug combination prevents infections, together with interferon-gamma?
nodes.note: Interferon-gamma boosts the phagocyte function that remains. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only cure.

nodes.q: His failure to kill Staphylococcus aureus could suggest myeloperoxidase deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Dye test turns blue (normal); usually healthy**, with occasional Candida infections, mainly in people with diabetes
**Dye test stays colorless + abscesses with Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus** from early infancy

nodes.note: The trap: both have normal engulfment and a defect in the oxidative killing pathway. Myeloperoxidase deficiency is common and mostly harmless, and it can give a falsely abnormal dihydrorhodamine test, but the nitroblue tetrazolium test is normal because superoxide is still made.

nodes.q: His recurrent infections could suggest Chediak-Higashi syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Partial albinism + giant granules in neutrophils** (lysosomal trafficking defect, LYST gene) + nerve damage; normal dye test
**Normal skin and hair color; normal-sized granules; colorless dye test**

nodes.q: His infections could suggest leukocyte adhesion deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Delayed separation of the umbilical cord + very high neutrophil count + infections without pus** (CD18 integrin defect)
**Thick pus in abscesses + normal neutrophil count + colorless dye test**

nodes.q: His abscesses could suggest hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Very high immunoglobulin E + eczema + coarse face + retained baby teeth + cold staphylococcal abscesses**
**Normal immunoglobulin E + warm, pus-filled abscesses + Aspergillus pneumonia**

nodes.q: His infections could suggest Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Eczema + low, small platelets with bleeding + infections with encapsulated bacteria**
**Normal platelet count, no eczema + staphylococcal and Aspergillus abscesses**

nodes.q: His infections could suggest DiGeorge syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low calcium (absent parathyroids) + heart defect + cleft palate and absent thymus**, with viral and fungal infections
**Normal calcium and heart examination + bacterial abscesses with pus**

nodes.q: His infections could suggest perinatal HIV infection. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Positive HIV test + falling CD4 count + opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis**
**Negative HIV test + normal lymphocyte counts + catalase-positive abscesses**

root.stem: A 27-year-old woman has had 7 days of sneezing, a blocked nose with clear watery discharge, and itchy, watery eyes. The same symptoms return every spring when she mows the lawn and walks in the park. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). Her nasal lining is pale and swollen with clear fluid, her sinuses are not tender, her throat is not red, and she has not used any nasal decongestant spray.
root.oneliner: 27F + 7 days of sneezing, blocked nose, clear watery discharge, itchy watery eyes + same every spring after mowing and walking in the park + afebrile + pale swollen nasal lining, clear fluid + no sinus tenderness, no red throat + no decongestant spray use
highlight: not used any nasal decongestant spray

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Inflammation of the nasal lining from an allergen. The clincher: **seasonal sneezing with itchy watery eyes and clear nasal discharge, no fever**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Hay fever and seasonal allergic rhinitis describe the same disease; grass and tree pollen are classic triggers.

nodes.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction causes it?
nodes.note: On first exposure, T helper 2 cells make interleukin-4, which switches B cells to make immunoglobulin E (IgE) that coats mast cells. On re-exposure the allergen cross-links the IgE on the mast cells, which release histamine within minutes.

nodes.q: Which mediator causes the sneezing, itching and watery discharge?
nodes.note: Histamine also increases vessel permeability and mucus secretion; leukotrienes add to the congestion.

nodes.q: Which property makes first-generation H1 blockers such as diphenhydramine sedating, unlike loratadine or cetirizine?
nodes.note: First-generation agents are lipid-soluble and also block muscarinic receptors (dry mouth, urinary retention), so they are avoided in older adults.

nodes.q: Which cell type is most increased in her nasal secretions?
nodes.note: Mast-cell mediators and interleukin-5 from T helper 2 cells recruit eosinophils for the late-phase reaction, so eosinophils build up in the secretions. Mast cells start the reaction but stay fixed in the tissue; basophils are few.

nodes.q: Which two other conditions complete the atopic triad with her rhinitis?
nodes.note: Together they make the atopic triad; the shared basis is IgE-driven T helper 2 inflammation.

nodes.q: Which type of drug relieves the nasal congestion in the short term?
nodes.a: Alpha-adrenergic agonist (for example pseudoephedrine or oxymetazoline)
nodes.note: They constrict nasal mucosal vessels through alpha-1 receptors. Topical forms should be limited to about 3 days, or rebound congestion follows (rhinitis medicamentosa).

nodes.q: Which drug is first-line for persistent symptoms?
nodes.note: Non-sedating oral antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine) help sneezing and itching but not congestion as well. Avoiding the allergen helps most.

nodes.q: Her symptoms could suggest a viral cold. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever + sore throat + thick yellow discharge that resolves within about 10 days**; red nasal lining; not seasonal
**Clear watery discharge + itchy eyes + same season each year + pale swollen lining**; no fever

nodes.note: The trap: both cause sneezing, a blocked nose and watery eyes.

nodes.q: Her blocked nose could suggest vasomotor rhinitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Triggered by temperature change, strong smells or smoke; no itching and no eosinophils** in the secretions
**Seasonal pollen trigger + itchy watery eyes + eosinophils in the secretions**

nodes.q: Her congestion could suggest rhinitis medicamentosa. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Rebound congestion after more than a few days of topical decongestant spray**; red, swollen lining; no seasonal pattern
**No decongestant use + seasonal pollen exposure + sneezing and itchy eyes**

nodes.q: Her watery eyes could suggest allergic conjunctivitis alone. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Itchy red eyes with stringy discharge and no nasal symptoms**
**Sneezing and nasal congestion with clear discharge**, with the eye symptoms as part of the same picture

root.stem: A 16-year-old boy develops swollen lips and face, a hoarse voice and noisy breathing a few hours after a tooth extraction. Since childhood he has had episodes of painless, firm swelling of his hands and feet with no hives and no itching, and he has had attacks of crampy abdominal pain with diarrhea and no fever. His mother has had similar swelling. Antihistamines and glucocorticoids have never helped. He takes no regular medicines, his skin is clear, his urine is a normal color, and he has no history of frequent infections. Serum C4 and C2 are low and C3 is normal.
root.oneliner: 16M + facial swelling and noisy breathing hours after a tooth extraction + lifelong painless firm swelling of hands and feet, no hives, no itching + crampy abdominal pain with diarrhea, no fever + mother similar + antihistamines and steroids never helped + no regular medicines, clear skin, normal urine color, no frequent infections + low C4 and C2, normal C3
highlight: crampy abdominal pain with diarrhea and no fever
His mother has had similar swelling
Antihistamines and glucocorticoids have never helped
C4 and C2 are low and C3 is normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Episodes of swelling from bradykinin, not histamine. The clincher: **recurrent painless swelling without hives + abdominal attacks + low C4 and C2 with a normal C3 + family history**, often set off by trauma such as dental work.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease; the exam often words it as 'decreased C1 esterase inhibitors'.

nodes.q: Which vasoactive peptide builds up and causes the swelling?
nodes.note: Without C1 inhibitor, kallikrein is not held in check and keeps cutting kininogen into bradykinin, which makes vessels leak. Histamine is not involved, which is why antihistamines fail.

nodes.q: How is the disease inherited?
nodes.note: The mother is affected too. About one quarter of cases are new mutations.

nodes.q: Which complement level is the best screening test, even between attacks?
nodes.note: Uncontrolled activated C1 uses up C4 and C2, so both are low while C3 stays normal. A low C1 inhibitor level or function confirms it.

nodes.q: What causes the abdominal pain and diarrhea?
nodes.note: Attacks can mimic an acute abdomen, and many patients have had unneeded surgery.

nodes.q: Which site of swelling can kill?
nodes.note: Dental work, throat procedures, trauma and stress are triggers. Swelling of the tongue or voice box needs early securing of the airway.

nodes.q: Which replacement product treats an acute attack?
nodes.note: Alternatives are the bradykinin B2 receptor blocker icatibant and the kallikrein inhibitor ecallantide; fresh frozen plasma if nothing else is available. Epinephrine, antihistamines and glucocorticoids do not work. Secure the airway early for laryngeal swelling.

nodes.q: Which drugs given long term raise liver production of C1 inhibitor?
nodes.note: They cut the number of attacks. Side effects are virilization and liver toxicity, so they are avoided in children and pregnancy; newer options are C1 inhibitor prophylaxis and lanadelumab.

nodes.q: Which antihypertensive drug class must he avoid because it blocks the breakdown of bradykinin?
nodes.note: ACE normally breaks down bradykinin. Estrogen-containing pills also trigger attacks.

nodes.q: His facial swelling could suggest allergic angioedema. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hives and itching within minutes of an allergen**; normal C4; responds quickly to epinephrine, antihistamines and glucocorticoids
**No hives, no itching + low C4 + no response to epinephrine or antihistamines** + family history

nodes.note: The trap: both cause lip and face swelling that can close the airway.

nodes.q: His swelling could suggest angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor angioedema. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Taking an ACE inhibitor (often an older adult or Black patient) + normal C4 and C2**; no childhood attacks or family history
**Takes no regular medicines + attacks since childhood + low C4 and C2**

nodes.q: His abdominal pain could suggest acute intermittent porphyria. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Abdominal pain with dark urine, nerve and psychiatric symptoms, and raised urine porphobilinogen**; no swelling
**Abdominal pain with swelling episodes, normal urine color, and low C4 and C2**

nodes.q: His abdominal attacks could suggest familial Mediterranean fever. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever with serositis (abdominal or chest pain) lasting 1 to 3 days; Mediterranean ancestry; defective pyrin protein**; normal complement
**Attacks without fever + swelling of skin or airway + low C4 and C2**

title: Major histocompatibility complex class II deficiency

root.stem: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of fever and a severe wet cough, after 2 months of persistent diarrhea. His breathing rate is 64/min and crackles are heard over all lung fields. A silver stain of lung washings shows round cysts. His parents are first cousins. A human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) test is negative in him and in his mother. Blood tests show a normal total lymphocyte count, low levels of all immunoglobulin classes, and no human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DR on his lymphocytes. His calcium level is normal and heart sounds are normal.
root.oneliner: 6-month-old boy + fever, wet cough, fast breathing, crackles in all lung fields + 2 months of diarrhea + silver stain shows round cysts + parents first cousins + HIV negative + normal lymphocyte count + low immunoglobulins + no HLA-DR on lymphocytes + normal calcium and heart
highlight: silver stain of lung washings shows round cysts
negative in him and in his mother
low levels of all immunoglobulin classes
no human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DR on his lymphocytes
calcium level is normal and heart sounds are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II deficiency
nodes.note: A primary immunodeficiency in which cells cannot display MHC class II molecules. The clincher: **an infant with an opportunistic infection + no HLA-DR on lymphocytes + a normal total lymphocyte count**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which genes fail to be switched on?
nodes.a: The MHC class II genes (HLA-DR, DP, DQ), because regulators such as CIITA or the RFX proteins are mutated
nodes.note: The mutation is in the transcription factors that activate the class II genes, not in the class II genes themselves.

nodes.q: Which T-cell population is markedly decreased?
nodes.note: CD4 cells are selected in the thymus on MHC class II molecules, so without them few mature. CD8 cells are normal because MHC class I is intact. Dendritic cells, monocytes and neutrophils are present, though dendritic cells and monocytes lack MHC class II.

nodes.q: Why are his immunoglobulin levels low?
nodes.a: B cells get no help from CD4 helper T cells
nodes.note: Antigen-presenting cells cannot show antigen to CD4 cells, so B cells do not switch class or make antibody.

nodes.q: How is the disease inherited?
nodes.note: Common in North African families, and consanguinity (first-cousin parents) raises the risk.

nodes.q: Which organism does the silver stain show?
nodes.note: A yeast-like fungus that appears as round or cup-shaped cysts on silver stain, causing pneumonia in cellular immune deficiency.

nodes.q: Which treatment is the only cure?
nodes.note: Until then: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis against Pneumocystis and immunoglobulin replacement for the antibody deficiency. Without transplantation most children die in early childhood.

nodes.q: His low CD4 cells and Pneumocystis could suggest perinatal HIV infection. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Positive HIV test in the infant, usually with a mother who has HIV**; HLA-DR is present on lymphocytes
**Negative HIV tests + no HLA-DR on lymphocytes + first-cousin parents**

nodes.note: The trap: both give Pneumocystis pneumonia in infancy with low CD4 helper T cells.

nodes.q: His infections could suggest severe combined immunodeficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Very low T-cell count (lymphopenia) with absent thymic shadow**; HLA molecules are present
**Normal total lymphocyte count; only CD4 cells low; HLA-DR absent**

nodes.q: His low T cells could suggest DiGeorge syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low calcium + heart defect + cleft palate and absent thymus**; HLA-DR is present
**Normal calcium and heart + no HLA-DR + severe diarrhea**

nodes.q: His Pneumocystis pneumonia could suggest hyper-IgM syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High or normal immunoglobulin M with low immunoglobulins G, A and E** (CD40 ligand defect on T cells, X-linked); HLA-DR is present
**All immunoglobulin classes low + no HLA-DR**; autosomal recessive

nodes.q: His absent HLA molecules could suggest MHC class I deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.a: MHC class I deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome type I)
split.note: **Low CD8 cells + no HLA-A, B, C; milder course with sinus and lung bacterial infections and skin granulomas**
**Low CD4 cells + no HLA-DR; severe opportunistic infection in infancy**

root.stem: A 6-year-old girl has had enlarged lymph nodes in her neck, armpits and groin since infancy, and her spleen is palpable 8 cm below the rib margin. Over the past year she has had a sudden fall in hemoglobin with jaundice and a separate episode of low platelets with bruising. Her father had similar enlarged lymph nodes as a child. She has no rash, no joint pain and no diarrhea, her antinuclear antibodies are negative, and her blood sugar is normal. Flow cytometry shows many T cells that carry neither CD4 nor CD8, her serum vitamin B12 is high, and a lymph node biopsy shows expanded paracortex with no malignant cells.
root.oneliner: 6F + lymph nodes in neck, armpits, groin since infancy + spleen 8 cm below rib margin + hemolysis with jaundice and low platelets with bruising + father similar as a child + no rash, joint pain or diarrhea, antinuclear antibodies negative + T cells with neither CD4 nor CD8 + high vitamin B12 + expanded node paracortex, no malignancy
highlight: father had similar enlarged lymph nodes
no rash, no joint pain and no diarrhea
expanded paracortex with no malignant cells

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A disorder of failed lymphocyte death, with lymph node and spleen enlargement plus autoimmune blood disease. The clincher: **chronic lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly + autoimmune cytopenias + T cells lacking both CD4 and CD8 (double-negative) + high vitamin B12**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which process fails in this disease?
nodes.note: Fas (CD95) on activated T and B cells binds Fas ligand and triggers caspase-8, ending the immune response. Without it, lymphocytes accumulate. Most cases are autosomal dominant FAS mutations, matching the father.

nodes.q: Which tolerance mechanism fails, so self-reactive lymphocytes are not removed?
nodes.note: The MRL/lpr mouse has a Fas defect and shows the same T-cell build-up and autoimmunity; exam questions word this as decreased responsiveness to clonal deletion signals. The defect is in killing of cells, not in faster T-cell division or stronger responses to antigen. In people, the main loss is activation-induced death of lymphocytes in the periphery.

nodes.q: Which type of T-cell receptor do her CD4-negative, CD8-negative T cells carry?

nodes.q: Why does it start 1 to 2 weeks after the first dose?

nodes.note: Same disease; exam options use either wording.

nodes.q: What is the lacy purplish net-like pattern on her legs called?
nodes.note: Sluggish flow in small skin vessels. Mild thrombocytopenia, as in her, is another common non-clot finding.

nodes.q: Which three antibody tests define it?
nodes.a: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies
nodes.note: Collectively called antiphospholipid antibodies. They are the cause of both the clots and the pregnancy losses.

nodes.q: Why is her partial thromboplastin time prolonged even though she is clotting?
nodes.a: The antibodies bind the phospholipid in the test reagent in the tube, but promote clotting in the body
nodes.note: The lupus anticoagulant is misnamed: it is a procoagulant in vivo. The prothrombin time can also be mildly prolonged in some patients.

nodes.q: Which laboratory test separates an inhibitor from a factor deficiency in her plasma?
nodes.a: The mixing study (her plasma mixed 1:1 with normal plasma)
nodes.note: A factor deficiency corrects on mixing; an inhibitor such as the lupus anticoagulant does not. The dilute Russell viper venom time is the confirmatory clotting test.

nodes.q: Which complication of her leg clot can kill her?
nodes.note: Sudden shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia. Unprovoked venous clots in a young woman should prompt testing for this syndrome.

nodes.q: Besides veins, which vessels can clot, causing stroke in a young patient?
nodes.note: Stroke, transient ischemic attack and myocardial infarction. Few inherited thrombophilias cause arterial clots, which helps point to this diagnosis.

nodes.q: Why is her rapid plasma reagin test positive with a negative treponemal test?
nodes.a: The reagin test uses cardiolipin as antigen, so the antibodies react with it (a biologic false positive)
nodes.note: A false-positive nontreponemal syphilis test can be the first clue.

nodes.q: What does the disease do to the placenta to cause recurrent fetal loss?
nodes.a: It causes thrombosis and infarction of the placental vessels
nodes.note: Typical losses: three or more before 10 weeks, or one fetal death at or after 10 weeks. It can also cause preeclampsia and premature birth.

nodes.q: Her lupus makes this the secondary form. What is it called when it occurs without another autoimmune disease?
nodes.note: Systemic lupus erythematosus is the disease most often behind the secondary form.

nodes.q: Which cardiac lesion can occur?
nodes.a: Libman-Sacks endocarditis (sterile warty vegetations, usually on the mitral valve)
nodes.note: Blood cultures are negative.

nodes.q: How is the diagnosis confirmed?
nodes.a: Positive antibodies on two tests at least 12 weeks apart
nodes.note: Transient positives occur with infection.

nodes.q: What is the long-term treatment after a venous thrombosis?
nodes.note: Heparin first, then warfarin. Direct oral anticoagulants are less effective in high-risk (triple-positive or arterial) disease.

nodes.q: Which anticoagulant replaces warfarin during pregnancy?
nodes.note: Warfarin crosses the placenta and is teratogenic; heparin does not cross the placenta.

nodes.q: Her clot and pregnancy losses could suggest factor V Leiden. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal partial thromboplastin time**; resistance to activated protein C; venous clots, often family history; commonest inherited thrombophilia
**Prolonged partial thromboplastin time not corrected by mixing + pregnancy losses + livedo reticularis**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause venous thrombosis and fetal loss in a young woman.

nodes.q: Her clots could suggest protein C deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal partial thromboplastin time**; warfarin-induced skin necrosis; family history
**Prolonged partial thromboplastin time that does not correct + antiphospholipid antibodies**

nodes.q: Her clots could suggest protein S deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal partial thromboplastin time**; low free protein S; family history; warfarin skin necrosis
**Prolonged partial thromboplastin time + false-positive reagin test**

nodes.q: Her clots could suggest antithrombin deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Heparin resistance**: partial thromboplastin time barely rises with heparin; normal baseline
**Prolonged baseline partial thromboplastin time not corrected by mixing**

nodes.q: Her clots could suggest the prothrombin G20210A mutation. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal partial thromboplastin time**; high prothrombin level; venous clots, family history
**Prolonged partial thromboplastin time not corrected by mixing**

nodes.q: Her clots could suggest a high factor VIII level. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Shortened partial thromboplastin time** (factor VIII is in the intrinsic pathway); venous clots
**Prolonged partial thromboplastin time**

nodes.q: Her clots could suggest dysfibrinogenemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Prolonged thrombin time**; can cause bleeding or thrombosis; abnormal fibrinogen function
**Normal thrombin time + prolonged partial thromboplastin time that does not correct**

root.stem: A 3-year-old boy has had eczema since infancy and repeated ear and lung infections with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. He bruises easily, has petechiae on his legs and had blood in his stool, and he bled for hours after a minor cut. His mother's brother died in childhood from bleeding. His platelet count is 30,000/mm3 and the platelets look small on the smear. Serum immunoglobulin M is low, immunoglobulins A and E are high, and immunoglobulin G is normal.
root.oneliner: 3M + eczema since infancy + recurrent ear and lung infections with encapsulated bacteria + easy bruising, petechiae, bloody stool, prolonged bleeding after a cut + mother's brother died of bleeding in childhood + platelets 30,000/mm3, small on smear + low IgM, high IgA and IgE, normal IgG
highlight: bled for hours after a minor cut
mother's brother died in childhood from bleeding
platelets look small on the smear
immunoglobulin M is low, immunoglobulins A and E are high

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An X-linked immunodeficiency. The clincher: **the triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and recurrent infections in a boy**.

nodes.q: Which pattern of inheritance explains his affected maternal uncle?
nodes.note: Mothers are carriers; boys are affected.

nodes.q: Which cellular process is defective because of the faulty WAS protein?
nodes.a: Actin cytoskeleton reorganisation in white cells and platelets
nodes.note: The WAS gene is on the X chromosome. Abnormal actin means poor cell movement, poor immune synapse formation, and small, short-lived platelets.

nodes.q: Which term names his platelet finding?
nodes.note: A low count of small platelets: petechiae, bruising, bloody stools and a prolonged bleeding time. The small platelets are also cleared early by the spleen.

nodes.q: Which bleeding complication is the most feared in these children?
nodes.note: Even minor head injury can cause it.

nodes.q: Why do encapsulated bacteria infect him even though his immunoglobulin G is normal?
nodes.a: He makes poor antibody responses to polysaccharide antigens
nodes.note: Typical pattern: low immunoglobulin M (IgM), high immunoglobulin A (IgA) and E (IgE), normal or slightly low immunoglobulin G (IgG). Hence otitis media and pneumonia with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. T-cell function also declines with age.

nodes.q: Which cancer is the long-term risk?
nodes.note: Often extranodal, even in the gut, and can appear in young adults. Autoimmune disease (especially autoimmune hemolytic anemia) is also more frequent.

nodes.q: What is the definitive treatment?
nodes.note: Supportive care: immunoglobulin replacement, infection prophylaxis, platelet transfusions (irradiated), and splenectomy can raise the platelet count.

nodes.q: His recurrent bacterial infections could suggest Bruton agammaglobulinemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Absent B cells and all immunoglobulins very low**; infections start after 6 months of age; no eczema, platelets normal
**Eczema + small platelets + low IgM with high IgA and E**; B cells present

nodes.note: The trap: both are X-linked boys with encapsulated bacterial infections.

nodes.q: His infections could suggest common variable immunodeficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Adolescents or adults; low IgG and IgA with normal B-cell count**; poor vaccine response; autoimmunity and lymphoma
**Boy in early childhood; eczema; small platelets; high IgA**

nodes.q: His immunoglobulin results could suggest selective immunoglobulin A deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Absent immunoglobulin A with normal immunoglobulin G and M**; often asymptomatic; no thrombocytopenia
**High immunoglobulin A and E + low IgM + thrombocytopenia**

nodes.q: His T-cell problems could suggest DiGeorge syndrome (thymic hypoplasia). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hypocalcemic seizures + heart defect + absent thymus + cleft palate**; 22q11 deletion; platelets normal
**Eczema + thrombocytopenia with small platelets**; X-linked

nodes.q: His infections and cancer risk could suggest acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Positive human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) test + low CD4 count**; opportunistic infections; no lifelong eczema or small platelets
**Lifelong eczema + small platelets, from birth, in a boy**; HIV test negative

nodes.q: His lymphoma could suggest Sjogren syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Dry eyes and dry mouth in a middle-aged woman + anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies**; marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma of the parotid; normal platelets
**Boy with eczema since infancy + small platelets + low IgM**

nodes.q: His eczema and infections could suggest hyperimmunoglobulin E (Job) syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Cold staphylococcal abscesses + retained primary teeth + very high IgE**; platelets normal
**Bleeding + small platelets + low IgM**
