root.stem: A 33-year-old woman has had frequent sinus infections and loose stools since childhood, and stool testing once found Giardia lamblia. A blood test for celiac disease that measures immunoglobulin A antibodies was negative, but a small-bowel biopsy showed flattened villi. Last year, within minutes of a blood transfusion after childbirth, she developed hives, wheezing and low blood pressure. Her serum immunoglobulin A is undetectable, while immunoglobulin G and M are normal and her B-cell count is normal.
root.oneliner: 33F + sinus infections and loose stools since childhood + Giardia once + negative celiac IgA antibody test, flattened villi on biopsy + hives, wheezing and low blood pressure within minutes of a transfusion + undetectable IgA, normal IgG and IgM + normal B-cell count
highlight: negative, but a small-bowel biopsy showed flattened villi
within minutes of a blood transfusion
hives, wheezing and low blood pressure
immunoglobulin G and M are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common primary immunodeficiency. The clincher: **very low serum IgA with normal immunoglobulin G (IgG) and M (IgM), plus anaphylaxis to blood products**.

nodes.q: What is the defect in the B cells?
nodes.a: They fail to mature into IgA-secreting plasma cells
nodes.note: B-cell numbers are normal. Secretory IgA at mucosal surfaces is lacking.

nodes.q: Which body surfaces lose their main antibody defence, explaining her sinus and gut infections?
nodes.note: Sinopulmonary bacteria and Giardia. Many patients have no symptoms.

nodes.q: Which immune mediator explains her reaction to the transfusion?
nodes.a: Preformed anti-IgA antibodies reacting with donor IgA in the plasma
nodes.note: An anaphylactic reaction: she sees the donor IgA as foreign. The anti-IgA antibodies are often IgG (sometimes IgE). It can follow fresh frozen plasma, platelets or whole blood, from minutes to a couple of hours after.

nodes.q: Which products avoid the reaction in future?
nodes.a: Washed red cells or plasma from IgA-deficient donors
nodes.note: Epinephrine treats the acute reaction.

nodes.q: Why was her celiac antibody test falsely negative?
nodes.a: The standard test measures IgA antibodies, which she cannot make
nodes.note: Celiac disease is more common in IgA deficiency. Use IgG-based tests or biopsy.

nodes.q: Besides celiac disease, which broad group of diseases is more common in her?
nodes.note: For example lupus and rheumatoid arthritis; atopy is also more common. A few progress to common variable immunodeficiency.

nodes.q: Her recurrent infections could suggest common variable immunodeficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low IgG as well as IgA**; poor vaccine response; granulomas, autoimmunity and lymphoma
**Only IgA is absent; IgG and IgM are normal**

nodes.q: Her infections could suggest Bruton agammaglobulinemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Boys; absent B cells; all immunoglobulins low**; severe infections after 6 months
**Normal B-cell count; only IgA low; often mild**

nodes.q: Her reaction could suggest transfusion-related acute lung injury. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Respiratory distress with non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema within 6 hours**; fever, no hives
**Hives + wheezing + low blood pressure within minutes**; anaphylaxis

nodes.q: Her low blood pressure minutes after a transfusion could suggest an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, flank pain, red-brown urine (hemoglobinuria) and a positive direct Coombs test** from ABO-incompatible red cells; no hives or wheeze
**Hives + wheezing + low blood pressure** with a compatible crossmatch; undetectable IgA

nodes.note: The trap: both start within minutes and drop the blood pressure. Hives and wheeze point to anaphylaxis, not hemolysis.

image_prompts.root: Soft pastel teaching picture of an IgA antibody dimer missing from a mucosal surface of the gut and sinus, with a bag of donor plasma carrying IgA being attacked by the patient's antibodies. No text.

root.stem: A 9-year-old girl has had an unsteady, wide-based gait that has worsened since she was 3 years old. Since age 5 she has had small dilated blood vessels on the whites of her eyes and on her ears. She has had many sinus and lung infections. Her intelligence is normal and she has no heart disease or foot deformity. Her sister has the same illness, and her parents are healthy. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is raised and immunoglobulin A is low.
root.oneliner: 9F + gait unsteady, worse since age 3 + dilated small vessels on eyes and ears since 5 + recurrent sinus and lung infections + normal intelligence, no heart disease, no foot deformity + affected sister, healthy parents + raised alpha-fetoprotein + low immunoglobulin A
highlight: small dilated blood vessels on the whites of her eyes
no heart disease or foot deformity
Her sister has the same illness

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A DNA-repair disorder. The clincher: **progressive cerebellar ataxia from early childhood + telangiectasias of eyes and ears + recurrent sinopulmonary infections**, with a raised alpha-fetoprotein as a supporting clue.

nodes.q: Which gene is mutated?
nodes.a: ATM (ataxia telangiectasia mutated) gene on chromosome 11
nodes.note: It codes a kinase that senses DNA damage.

nodes.q: Which pattern of inheritance fits her affected sister and healthy parents?
Which process fails in her cells?
nodes.a: Repair of double-strand DNA breaks (the ATM kinase normally detects them and halts the cell cycle)
nodes.note: Cells are very sensitive to ionizing radiation, and breaks lead to translocations involving the immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor genes.

nodes.q: Which cells degenerate in the cerebellum?
nodes.note: Cerebellar atrophy, especially the vermis, causes the ataxia.

nodes.q: Besides her low immunoglobulin A, which arm of immunity is also deficient?
nodes.a: T cells (from a small, underdeveloped thymus)
nodes.note: Immunoglobulin G2 and E are often low too. Together these explain the sinus and lung infections and later bronchiectasis.

nodes.q: Which group of cancers is she at high risk of?
nodes.a: Lymphoid cancers (lymphomas, including Hodgkin lymphoma, and leukemias)
nodes.note: Often the cause of death with lung disease.

nodes.q: Which exposure should be minimised in her care?
nodes.note: Her cells cannot repair the breaks; radiotherapy is poorly tolerated. No cure; supportive care.

nodes.q: Her ataxia could suggest Friedreich ataxia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **GAA repeat in the frataxin gene + hypertrophic cardiomyopathy + diabetes + scoliosis and pes cavus + absent reflexes**; no telangiectasias
**Telangiectasias + recurrent infections + raised alpha-fetoprotein + no heart or foot deformity**

nodes.note: The trap: both are autosomal recessive childhood ataxias.

nodes.q: Her DNA repair defect could suggest xeroderma pigmentosum. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Extreme sun sensitivity + freckling + early skin cancers**; defective nucleotide excision repair of UV damage
**Ataxia + telangiectasias + immunodeficiency + radiation sensitivity**; double-strand break repair

nodes.q: Her cancer risk could suggest Bloom syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Short stature + sun-sensitive facial rash + high sister chromatid exchange**; BLM helicase
**Ataxia + telangiectasias**; normal stature

root.stem: A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has had recurrent thrush and a Candida skin infection. He has had few bacterial infections in his life. His neutrophil count is normal, and an automated blood count analyzer that stains neutrophils for peroxidase reports that his neutrophils lack peroxidase. A nitroblue tetrazolium test is normal.
root.oneliner: 52M + poorly controlled diabetes + recurrent thrush and Candida skin infection + few bacterial infections + normal neutrophil count + neutrophils lack peroxidase staining + normal nitroblue tetrazolium test
highlight: recurrent thrush and a Candida skin infection

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common inherited phagocyte disorder, usually autosomal recessive and mild. The clincher: **neutrophils with no peroxidase and no hypochlorous acid, with a normal oxidative burst test**.

nodes.q: Which product that kills microbes cannot be made?
nodes.note: Myeloperoxidase normally turns hydrogen peroxide and chloride into hypochlorous acid in the phagolysosome.

nodes.q: Why is the nitroblue tetrazolium test normal?
nodes.a: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase works and makes superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; the defect is downstream
nodes.note: Myeloperoxidase acts after NADPH oxidase.

nodes.q: Why does Candida in particular escape his neutrophils?
nodes.a: Killing of Candida depends heavily on the myeloperoxidase-hypochlorous acid system
nodes.note: Bacterial killing is slowed, but other oxygen-dependent and non-oxygen pathways compensate. Diabetes makes Candida infection more likely.

nodes.q: How severe is it compared with chronic granulomatous disease?
nodes.a: Much milder; most patients have no symptoms
nodes.note: Often found by chance on an automated blood count.

nodes.q: What treats the Candida infection?
nodes.a: An azole antifungal such as fluconazole, with better glucose control
nodes.note: Azoles block ergosterol synthesis in the fungal cell membrane. No specific therapy is needed otherwise.

nodes.q: His infections could suggest chronic granulomatous disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Abnormal oxidative burst test**; severe infections with catalase-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia, Aspergillus); granulomas
**Normal oxidative burst test + absent peroxidase**; mild; Candida

nodes.note: The trap: both leave neutrophils unable to kill ingested microbes efficiently.

nodes.q: His neutrophil defect could suggest Chediak-Higashi syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Giant granules in neutrophils + partial albinism + neuropathy**
**Normal granules; absent peroxidase staining**

nodes.q: His infections could suggest leukocyte adhesion deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Delayed cord separation + very high neutrophil count + no pus**; severe bacterial infections in infancy
**Normal neutrophil count; adult with Candida; absent peroxidase**

root.stem: A 52-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis C has had 3 weeks of fatigue and aching in her hands and knees. Raised, red-purple spots that do not blanch cover both shins, and she has numbness in her feet. Her blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg, her liver and spleen are enlarged, and urinalysis shows blood and protein. The rheumatoid factor is positive, serum C4 is low, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are negative, and hepatitis B surface antigen is negative.
root.oneliner: 52F + chronic hepatitis C + fatigue and hand and knee aching for 3 weeks + raised non-blanching red-purple spots on shins + numb feet + blood pressure 150/90 + enlarged liver and spleen + blood and protein in urine + positive rheumatoid factor + low C4 + negative antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and hepatitis B surface antigen
highlight: Raised, red-purple spots that do not blanch
hepatitis B surface antigen is negative

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A small-vessel vasculitis from immune complexes that precipitate in the cold. The clincher: **chronic hepatitis C + palpable purpura, arthralgia and fatigue (Meltzer triad) + positive rheumatoid factor with low C4**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same disease.

nodes.q: Which serum finding confirms it?
nodes.a: Cryoglobulins (proteins that precipitate when cooled and redissolve on warming)
nodes.note: This is the serum protein that is increased. The blood sample must be kept warm at 37 °C until the serum is separated, or the test can be falsely negative.

nodes.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction causes the vasculitis?
nodes.note: The complexes are immunoglobulin M (IgM) rheumatoid factor bound to polyclonal immunoglobulin G (IgG); they lodge in small vessels and activate complement.

nodes.q: Why is her C4 low?
nodes.a: The immune complexes consume it by activating the classical complement pathway
nodes.note: C4 is often very low with C3 less affected. Complement is never raised in this disease, a common wrong option.

nodes.q: How does her hepatitis C infection drive the disease?
nodes.a: Chronic stimulation of B cells, which make IgM rheumatoid factor against IgG
nodes.note: Hepatitis B, human immunodeficiency virus and connective tissue diseases are less common causes.

nodes.q: Which vessels are inflamed to cause the purpura?
nodes.note: The purpura is palpable because of inflammation in the vessel wall.

nodes.q: Which kidney disease explains the blood and protein in the urine?
nodes.note: Immune complexes deposit in the glomeruli; the kidney is a main cause of death.

nodes.q: What causes the numbness in her feet?
nodes.a: Peripheral neuropathy from vasculitis of the small vessels that supply nerves (vasa nervorum)
nodes.note: Usually a symmetric sensory neuropathy; mononeuritis multiplex can occur.

nodes.q: Which cancer is a long-term risk?
nodes.note: Chronic B-cell stimulation.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Treat the hepatitis C virus with direct-acting antivirals
nodes.note: Rituximab with corticosteroids for severe disease; plasmapheresis for life-threatening cases.

nodes.q: Her purpura and joint pain could suggest IgA vasculitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Children; abdominal pain after an upper respiratory infection; IgA deposits; normal complement**
**Adult with hepatitis C; cryoglobulins + low C4 + positive rheumatoid factor**

nodes.note: The trap: both give palpable purpura, joint pain and kidney disease.

nodes.q: Her vasculitis could suggest polyarteritis nodosa. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Medium-sized arteries; hepatitis B; kidney artery microaneurysms without glomerulonephritis; no cryoglobulins or low C4**
**Small vessels; hepatitis C; glomerulonephritis + palpable purpura**

nodes.q: Her joint pain and positive rheumatoid factor could suggest rheumatoid arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Symmetric erosive arthritis of small joints with morning stiffness**; anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies; no purpura
**Non-erosive arthralgia + palpable purpura + low C4 + hepatitis C**
